title: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and the Concept of Probability
topicTitle: Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle and concept of probability
notes: Werner Heisenberg (1927) showed that for a microscopic particle it is impossible to determine simultaneously and exactly both its position and its momentum: $\Delta x\cdot\Delta p\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$, or $\Delta x\cdot\Delta v\ge\frac{h}{4\pi m}$. Other conjugate pairs obey the same pattern: $\Delta E\cdot\Delta t\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$ and $\Delta L\cdot\Delta\theta\ge\frac{h}{4\pi}$.

To locate an electron we must 'illuminate' it with radiation of wavelength comparable to its size; such a photon collides with the electron and changes its momentum by an unknown amount, while using longer-wavelength radiation blurs the position. The disturbance is a property of matter, not an experimental defect — the γ-ray microscope is the standard illustration.

A definite orbit needs exact r and p simultaneously, which the principle forbids. The electron's location can only be described by a wave function ψ, where |ψ|² dV is the **probability** of finding the electron in volume dV — the electron-cloud or **orbital** picture. The radial probability peak for the 1s orbital lies at 0.529 Å: the same number Bohr obtained, now interpreted as a most-probable distance instead of a fixed radius.

• **Atomic stability and size:** an electron confined to a nucleus (Δx ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) would need Δp ≈ 10⁻¹⁹ kg m s⁻¹, i.e. KE of the order 10¹⁰ eV — impossible; hence electrons cannot sit inside nuclei and atoms are ≈10⁻¹⁰ m across, which also explains why the electron does not fall into the nucleus.
• **Natural line width:** an excited state living Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s has ΔE ≥ h/4πΔt, so spectral lines are broadened; the same relation explains tunnelling and virtual-particle processes.

• **Zero-point energy** of confined particles, resolution limits of electron microscopes, quantum-dot behaviour and NMR line widths all follow from the principle, and all quantum-mechanical predictions (average radii, orbital shapes) are probabilistic.

The relation matters only for microscopic particles — for a 1 g body the product is utterly negligible, so classical mechanics holds. It forbids *simultaneous* exact knowledge, not knowledge of one quantity: perfect momentum knowledge leaves position completely undefined. Interpretations differ (Copenhagen versus measurement-disturbance readings), so it is safest to state it as a property of quantum ensembles; it is not a statement about instrument precision and does not mean measurement is impossible.
confusion: ❌ The principle is due to clumsy instruments. ✅ It is fundamental; better instruments cannot beat h/4π.
❌ It says nothing about the electron can be known. ✅ Either quantity may be exact; only the *product* of uncertainties is bounded below.
❌ It applies equally to a moving cricket ball. ✅ For macroscopic bodies the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical physics applies.
❌ The principle proves electrons do not exist in atoms. ✅ It replaces fixed orbits by probability distributions (orbitals) described by |ψ|².
❌ ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π is a different law. ✅ It is the energy–time form of the same principle, explaining natural line broadening.

universalFacts: Heisenberg published the principle in 1927 and received the 1932 Nobel Prize in Physics.
ħ = h/2π = 1.054 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; the bound is often written Δx·Δp ≥ ħ/2.
The most probable distance of the 1s electron is 0.529 Å — the value Bohr called the first-orbit radius.
examples: **Problem:** Minimum velocity uncertainty for an electron localised within 10⁻¹⁰ m. **Solution:** Δv ≥ h/(4πmΔx) = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(4π × 9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ — comparable to the electron's own speed, so the orbit picture collapses.

**Problem:** Can an electron be confined in a nucleus of radius 10⁻¹⁵ m? **Solution:** Δp ≈ h/(4πΔx) ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻²⁰ kg m s⁻¹ → KE ≈ (Δp)²/2m ≈ 10¹⁰ eV, far beyond nuclear binding energies; β-particles are therefore created during decay, not stored in the nucleus.
importantNotes: Write both forms: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π and Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm — questions often ask about velocity.
Use the principle to justify atomic size (~10⁻¹⁰ m) and stability; these are standard 3-mark applications.
State clearly that the limit is fundamental, not instrumental.
summary: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle (1927) states that for a microscopic particle position and momentum cannot both be determined exactly: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, or Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm, with the conjugate forms ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π and ΔL·Δθ ≥ h/4π. The cause is not clumsy instruments but physics: to locate an electron you must illuminate it with radiation of comparable wavelength, and that photon disturbs its momentum. The consequence is the concept of probability — the electron is described by a wave function ψ with |ψ|² as the probability density, so 0.529 Å reappears as the most probable distance of the 1s electron rather than a fixed radius. Numerically, an electron confined to 10⁻¹⁰ m has Δv ≈ 5.8 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹, so no definite orbit exists, and confinement to a nucleus would demand ≈10⁹ eV, proving electrons are not nuclear constituents.
importantConcepts: Position–momentum form Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π, or Δx·Δv ≥ h/4πm for velocity
Conjugate forms: energy–time ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π (natural line width) and ΔL·Δθ ≥ h/4π
Physical reason: illuminating the electron to locate it disturbs its momentum — a fundamental, not instrumental, limit
Probability concept: wave function ψ, probability density |ψ|², electron cloud and the most probable radius 0.529 Å for 1s
Applications: atomic size and stability, line broadening, zero-point energy, resolution limits of electron microscopes
importantStatements: Only the product of the uncertainties is bounded; either quantity alone may be exact.
The limit is a property of nature, so no better instrument can beat h/4π.
A definite Bohr orbit gives Δx ≈ 0 and Δp ≈ 0 at once, so Δx·Δp → 0, which is impossible.
An electron confined to 10⁻¹⁵ m would need Δp ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁸ kg m s⁻¹ and a KE of order 10⁹–10¹⁰ eV, far above nuclear binding energies.
For macroscopic bodies the uncertainty product is negligible, so classical mechanics remains valid.

ΔE·Δt ≥ h/4π explains why spectral lines have a natural width, since Δt ≈ 10⁻⁸ s.
The 1s most probable distance is 0.529 Å — Bohr's radius reinterpreted as probability.

specialNotes: The principle forbids simultaneous exact knowledge, not knowledge of one quantity — perfect p leaves position undefined.
Interpretations differ (Copenhagen versus measurement-disturbance), so state it as a property of quantum ensembles.
It does not mean measurement is impossible, only that conjugate quantities cannot both be sharp.
